CLINICAL DENTAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE: ENDODONTIC IRRIGATION,
DISINFECTION, AND FLARE-UP MANAGEMENT
American Association of Endodontists Reference Protocol
Guideline Code: ENDO-IRRIG-2024-V3
1. PRIMARY IRRIGATING SOLUTIONS & MECHANISM OF ACTION
A. Sodium Hypochlorite (NaOCl) - 2.5% to 5.25%
- Indication: Gold standard primary antimicrobial and organic tissue solvent. - Properties: Dissolves vital and necrotic pulp tissue remnants, disrupts biofilm, and eliminates Enterococcus faecalis.

- Application Protocol: Continual gentle replenishment throughout root canal instrumentation. Deliver at least 2 mL per canal
between instrument changes using a 30-gauge side-vented needle placed 1-2 mm short of working length. - Heating NaOCl (to 45°C - 60°C) or ultrasonic activation (passive ultrasonic irrigation - PUI) substantially enhances
dissolution rate and tissue penetration into lateral canals and isthmuses. - Hypochlorite Accident Prevention:
* NEVER inject NaOCl with wedged needle.

* Always verify needle moves freely in the canal space. * If accident occurs (sudden excruciating pain, rapid facial swelling, profuse interstitial bleeding): immediately cease
irrigation, inject local anesthetic for pain, prescribe analgesics, cold compresses first 24 hours followed by warm
compresses, and antibiotic coverage (e.g., Amoxicillin 500 mg TID or Clindamycin for penicillin-allergic patients). B.

Ethylenediaminetetraacetic Acid (EDTA) - 17% Solution
- Indication: Chelating agent for removal of the inorganic smear layer created during mechanical rotary or hand
instrumentation. - Protocol: After completing mechanical preparation and NaOCl irrigation, rinse canal with 1-2 mL of 17% EDTA for 1
minute. - Rationale: Opens dentinal tubules to permit deep penetration of root canal sealers and subsequent disinfection agents.

- Important Timing: Do not leave EDTA in canal for more than 1 to 2 minutes as prolonged exposure can cause excessive
dentinal erosion and tooth weakening. C. Chemical Interaction Warning: NaOCl + Chlorhexidine Gluconate (CHX)
- WARNING: Direct mixing of Sodium Hypochlorite (NaOCl) with Chlorhexidine (CHX 2%) produces an insoluble
brownish-orange precipitate (Parachloroaniline - PCA). - PCA is cytotoxic, occludes dentinal tubules, and stains the tooth structure.

- Strict Protocol: If using 2% CHX as a final antimicrobial flush, ALWAYS thoroughly rinse and dry the canal with sterile
saline or sterile water between NaOCl and CHX applications to prevent precipitate formation. 2. INTRACANAL MEDICAMENT
- Calcium Hydroxide Paste [Ca(OH)2]:
* Standard inter-appointment medicament for teeth with apical periodontitis or necrotic pulps. * High pH (~12.5) provides potent antimicrobial coverage and denatures bacterial lipopolysaccharides (endotoxins).

[Page 2]
* Minimum recommended intracanal duration: 7 to 14 days. 3. EMERGENCY ENDODONTIC FLARE-UP MANAGEMENT
- Characterized by severe pain and/or swelling starting a few hours or days following endodontic intervention. - Immediate Steps:
1. Re-evaluate occlusion and relieve any hyper-occlusal contact points immediately. 2. Re-open tooth under rubber dam isolation, re-irrigate thoroughly with copious warm NaOCl, dry with sterile paper points. 3. Re-medicate with Ca(OH)2 paste and place secure double seal (Cavit / IRM + Glass Ionomer). 4.

Pharmacological Pain Management: Combine Ibuprofen 600 mg + Acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours for synergistic
analgesia. 5. Antibiotics are NOT indicated for localized irreversible pulpitis or symptomatic apical periodontitis unless systemic
symptoms (fever > 38°C, malaise, lymphadenopathy, or spreading facial cellulitis) are present.

CLINICAL DENTAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE: LOCAL ANESTHESIA
DOSING, CALCULATIONS, AND TOXICITY PROTOCOL
Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery & Dental Therapeutics
Guideline Code: DENT-ANESTH-2024-V2
1. COMMONLY USED LOCAL ANESTHETICS IN DENTISTRY
A. Lidocaine HCl 2% with 1:100,000 Epinephrine
- Concentration: 2% lidocaine = 20 mg/mL. Standard dental cartridge contains 1.8 mL = 36 mg of lidocaine hydrochloride. - Vasoconstrictor: Epinephrine 1:100,000 = 0.01 mg/mL = 0.018 mg epinephrine per 1.8 mL cartridge.

- Maximum Recommended Dose (MRD) - Healthy Adult: 4.4 mg/kg (or 2.0 mg/lb), with an absolute maximum ceiling of 300
mg (approximately 8.3 cartridges for a 70 kg adult). - Pediatric MRD: 4.4 mg/kg strictly calculated based on actual body weight. * Example: For a 20 kg child: 20 kg x 4.4 mg/kg = 88 mg max lidocaine. 88 mg / 36 mg per cartridge = 2.4 cartridges
maximum. * Example: For a 30 kg child: 30 kg x 4.4 mg/kg = 132 mg max lidocaine. 132 mg / 36 mg per cartridge = 3.6 cartridges
maximum. - Onset: 2 to 4 minutes.

Pulpal anesthesia duration: 60 minutes. Soft tissue anesthesia: 3 to 5 hours. B. Articaine HCl 4% with 1:100,000 or 1:200,000 Epinephrine
- Concentration: 4% articaine = 40 mg/mL. A 1.8 mL cartridge contains 72 mg of articaine hydrochloride. - Maximum Recommended Dose: 7.0 mg/kg (3.2 mg/lb) up to an absolute maximum ceiling of 500 mg. - High lipid solubility provides superior bone penetration (useful for mandibular buccal infiltration in molars).

- Caution: Higher reported risk of paresthesia with mandibular nerve blocks; recommended primarily for maxillary infiltration
and mandibular infiltration. C. Mepivacaine 3% Plain (Without Vasoconstrictor)
- Concentration: 3% mepivacaine = 30 mg/mL = 54 mg per 1.8 mL cartridge. - Maximum Recommended Dose: 4.4 mg/kg, absolute max 300 mg (approximately 5.5 cartridges). - Indication: Patients for whom epinephrine is contraindicated (severe cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled hyperthyroidism,
sulfite allergy). 2.

VASOCONSTRICTOR LIMITS IN MEDICALLY COMPROMISED PATIENTS
- Healthy Patient (ASA I): Maximum epinephrine dose per appointment is 0.2 mg (up to 11 cartridges of 1:100,000). - Cardiac / Cardiovascular Compromise (ASA III or IV):
* Maximum epinephrine dose per appointment is restricted to 0.04 mg (equivalent to MAXIMUM TWO cartridges of
1:100,000 epinephrine). * Always aspirate in two planes before injection to prevent accidental intravascular administration.

* Contraindicated in patients with unstable angina, recent myocardial infarction (< 6 months), refractory arrhythmias, or
uncontrolled hypertension (BP > 180/110 mmHg).

[Page 2]
3. SIGNS OF LOCAL ANESTHETIC SYSTEMIC TOXICITY (LAST)
- Early CNS Excitation: Metallic taste in mouth, circumoral numbness, tinnitus, lightheadedness, restlessness, visual
disturbances, slurred speech. - Progression: Muscle twitching, tremors, generalized tonic-clonic seizures. - CNS & Cardiovascular Collapse: Respiratory depression, bradycardia, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiac
arrest. - Emergency Management:
1. Terminate dental procedure immediately. 2. Call Emergency Medical Services (911). 3.
Maintain airway, administer 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask. 4. In severe LAST with hemodynamic instability, administer 20% Intralipid emulsion (1.5 mL/kg initial bolus).

CONFIDENTIAL PATIENT DENTAL RECORD & CLINICAL ENCOUNTER
NOTE
Metro Dental Specialty Center - Electronic Health Record (EHR)
Chart Number: EHR-2024-9941
Encounter Date: September 12, 2024
Attending Dentist: Dr. Sarah Lin, DDS
Dental Assistant: Alex Rivera, RDA
1. PATIENT DEMOGRAPHICS
- Full Name: John Doe
- Date of Birth: March 14, 1982 (Age: 42 years)
- Biological Sex: Male
- Weight: 78 kg (172 lbs)
- Emergency Contact: Mary Doe (Spouse) - 555-019-2831
2.

MEDICAL HISTORY & SYSTEMIC ALERTS
- Systemic Conditions: Essential Hypertension (diagnosed 2019, controlled on Lisinopril 10 mg daily). - Medical Alerts / Drug Allergies:
* PENICILLIN ALLERGY: Severe anaphylactoid reaction with generalized urticaria and wheezing in 2018. Strictly avoid all
Penicillins, Amoxicillin, Augmentin, and Cephalosporins. Alternative recommended: Clindamycin 300 mg or Azithromycin
500 mg. * Latex sensitivity: Minor contact dermatitis. Use nitrile gloves and non-latex dental dam exclusively.

- Current Medications: Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily, Multivitamin. - ASA Physical Status Classification: ASA II (Mild systemic disease, well-controlled hypertension). - Vital Signs at Encounter: Blood Pressure 128/82 mmHg, Pulse 72 bpm, SpO2 99% on room air. 3.

DENTAL CHIEF COMPLAINT & HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
- Chief Complaint: "Severe throbbing pain and swelling on my lower left jaw since yesterday, and my tooth broke while
eating."
- History of Present Illness: Patient reports biting down on an olive pit 48 hours ago resulting in a loud crack in the lower left
molar region. Progressed to constant throbbing pain exacerbated by cold drinks and mastication. 4.

CLINICAL & RADIOGRAPHIC FINDINGS
- Tooth Involved: #19 (Mandibular Left First Molar)
- Visual Inspection: Extensive distal-occlusal composite restoration with visible vertical fracture line extending subgingivally
along the lingual aspect into the furcation. Deep caries beneath margins.

[Page 2]
- Periodontal Probing: Isolated 8 mm probing depth along the mid-lingual aspect directly tracing the fracture line. Surrounding sites probe 2 to 3 mm. Bleeding upon probing positive. - Periapical Radiograph & Bitewing: J-shaped radiolucency around mesial and distal roots indicative of combined
endodontic-periodontal communication. Furcation involvement Class II. The vertical root fracture is clinically non-restorable. - Diagnosis: Non-restorable Vertical Root Fracture with Acute Apical Abscess on Tooth #19. 5.

PROPOSED TREATMENT PLAN
- Phase 1: Surgical extraction of tooth #19 under local anesthesia (Lidocaine 2% with 1:100,000 epinephrine, max 2-3
cartridges). - Phase 2: Socket debridement and socket preservation with freeze-dried bone allograft (FDBA) + collagen membrane
(Bio-Gide) to maintain alveolar ridge height and width. - Phase 3: Delayed single endosseous titanium implant placement (3 to 4 months post-extraction healing) followed by
screw-retained ceramic crown restoration.

- Post-Operative Prescriptions & Instructions:
* Analgesia: Ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours alternating with Acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours PRN pain. * Antibiotic (if needed for spreading infection): Clindamycin 300 mg QID for 7 days (Penicillin allergy noted!). * Chlorhexidine 0.12% oral rinse BID starting 24 hours post-op. * Routine post-extraction precautions: 24 hours bite pressure, no straws, no spitting.

CLINICAL DENTAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE: PEDIATRIC DENTAL
TRAUMA & TOOTH AVULSION MANAGEMENT
International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) Reference Guidelines
Guideline Code: DENT-TRAUMA-2024-V2
1. GENERAL ASSESSMENT & TRIAGE
- Immediate Neurological & Medical Screen:
* Check for concussion, loss of consciousness, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or neck pain. If present, refer immediately to
emergency department. * Check tetanus immunization status.

If the patient has not had a booster within 5 years or wound is contaminated with
dirt/soil, administer tetanus prophylaxis within 48 hours. 2. TOOTH AVULSION PROTOCOLS
A. Primary Teeth (Deciduous Dentition) - AGES 0 TO 6 YEARS:
- CRITICAL RULE: NEVER REPLANT AN AVULSED PRIMARY TOOTH! - Replantation of primary teeth can damage the developing permanent tooth germ beneath the socket (causing enamel
hypoplasia, dilaceration, or arrest of permanent tooth eruption).

- Protocol: Confirm tooth has been completely expelled (take radiograph if aspirated or intruded). Reassure parents,
prescribe soft diet for 7-10 days, monitor for gingival healing. B. Permanent Teeth (Dentition in Children & Adults):
- Emergency First Aid at Scene of Injury:
* Hold tooth only by the crown; NEVER touch or scrape the root. * If dirty, rinse gently under cold running water for 10 seconds (do not scrub). * Immediately replant into the socket if possible, and have patient bite gently on a clean handkerchief or gauze.

- Storage & Transport Media (when immediate replantation not possible):
1. Hank's Balanced Salt Solution (HBSS) - Gold standard, maintains periodontal ligament (PDL) cell viability for up to 24
hours. 2. Cold Bovine Milk - Readily available, optimal osmolarity, keeps cells viable up to 6 hours. 3. Saliva (buccal vestibule or spit into a container) - Viable for 1-2 hours. 4. Physiological Saline. * WARNING: NEVER store avulsed tooth in tap water (hypotonic, causes rapid cell lysis).

- Clinical Treatment at Dental Office:
* Extra-oral dry time < 60 minutes:
- Rinse root gently with saline. Irrigate socket gently with saline to remove blood clot. - Replant tooth with gentle finger pressure.

[Page 2]
- Apply flexible splint (0.016" stainless steel wire with composite resin) for 2 WEEKS. - Rigid splinting is contraindicated (promotes replacement resorption / ankylosis). * Extra-oral dry time > 60 minutes:
- PDL cells are non-viable. Ankylosis and root resorption are inevitable. - Remove necrotic PDL tissue, soak in 2% sodium fluoride for 20 minutes to slow resorption. - Replant and place flexible splint for 4 WEEKS.

- Systemic Medications & Prophylaxis:
* Antibiotic Therapy:
- For children > 12 years / adults: Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days. - For children < 12 years (risk of tooth discoloration with tetracyclines): Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided TID for 7 days (or
Clindamycin if penicillin-allergic). * Chlorhexidine 0.12% mouth rinse BID for 2 weeks to assist oral hygiene. - Endodontic Follow-up:
* Teeth with closed apex: Initiate root canal therapy within 7 to 10 days after replantation (before splint removal) to prevent
inflammatory root resorption.

Place Ca(OH)2 paste. * Teeth with open apex (immature root): Monitor for revascularization; delay endodontics unless symptoms or radiographic
signs of necrosis appear.

CLINICAL DENTAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE: PERIODONTAL DIAGNOSIS,
STAGING, AND GRADING
American Academy of Periodontology (AAP) and European Federation of Periodontology (EFP)
Guideline Code: DENT-PERIO-2024-V1
1. PERIODONTAL STAGING (SEVERITY & EXTENT OF DISEASE)
- Stage I (Initial Periodontitis):
* Clinical Attachment Loss (CAL): 1 to 2 mm at site of greatest loss. * Radiographic Bone Loss (RBL): Coronal third (< 15% root length). * Probing Depth (PD): Max <= 4 mm. * Tooth Loss: No tooth loss due to periodontitis.

* Bone Loss Pattern: Mostly horizontal bone loss. - Stage II (Moderate Periodontitis):
* CAL: 3 to 4 mm. * RBL: Coronal third (15% to 33% root length). * Probing Depth: Max <= 5 mm. * Tooth Loss: No tooth loss due to periodontitis. * Bone Loss Pattern: Mostly horizontal. - Stage III (Severe Periodontitis with Potential for Additional Tooth Loss):
* CAL: >= 5 mm. * RBL: Extending to middle third of root or beyond (> 33%). * Probing Depth: >= 6 mm. * Tooth Loss: <= 4 teeth lost due to periodontitis.

* Complexity: Vertical bone loss >= 3 mm, furcation involvement Class II or III, moderate ridge defect. - Stage IV (Advanced Periodontitis with Potential for Dentition Loss):
* CAL: >= 5 mm. * RBL: Extending to middle third of root or beyond. * Tooth Loss: >= 5 teeth lost due to periodontitis. * Complexity: Severe masticatory dysfunction, secondary occlusal trauma, tooth mobility degree >= 2, severe ridge defects,
less than 20 remaining teeth (10 opposing pairs). 2.

PERIODONTAL GRADING (RATE OF PROGRESSION & SYSTEMIC MODIFIERS)
- Grade A (Slow Rate of Progression):
* Objective Evidence: No bone loss over 5 years; RBL/age ratio < 0.25. * Risk Factor Modifiers: Non-smoker, normoglycemic / non-diabetic. - Grade B (Moderate Rate of Progression):

[Page 2]
* Objective Evidence: < 2 mm bone loss over 5 years; RBL/age ratio 0.25 to 1.0. * Risk Factor Modifiers: Smoker < 10 cigarettes/day; HbA1c < 7.0% in diabetic patients. - Grade C (Rapid Rate of Progression):
* Objective Evidence: >= 2 mm bone loss over 5 years; RBL/age ratio > 1.0. * Risk Factor Modifiers: Smoker >= 10 cigarettes/day; HbA1c >= 7.0% in diabetic patients. 3.

TREATMENT PROTOCOLS & CLINICAL SEQUENCING
- Step 1: Periodontal health education, supragingival plaque control, chlorhexidine 0.12% rinse, smoking cessation
counseling, glycemic control coordination. - Step 2: Subgingival instrumentation (Scaling and Root Planing - SRP) using ultrasonic scalers and site-specific Gracey
curettes under local anesthesia.

- Step 3 (if residual pockets >= 6 mm persist after 6-8 weeks re-evaluation): Periodontal flap surgery, resective surgery, or
guided tissue regeneration (GTR) using bone grafts and barrier membranes. - Step 4: Supportive Periodontal Therapy (SPT) / Maintenance visits every 3 months.

CLINICAL DENTAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE: POST-EXTRACTION
SURGICAL PROTOCOL, BLEEDING CONTROL, AND DRY SOCKET
MANAGEMENT
Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery Clinical Protocols
Guideline Code: DENT-SURG-2024-V1
1. ROUTINE POST-EXTRACTION CARE & HEMOSTASIS
- Primary Hemostasis:
* Place sterile folded gauze directly over extraction socket. Instruct patient to apply firm, steady biting pressure for 30 to 45
minutes continuously.

* Avoid spitting, rinsing, drinking through straws, smoking, or vigorous exercise for 24 hours to prevent dislodging the initial
blood clot. * Ice packs applied externally (20 minutes on, 20 minutes off) for the first 24 hours to minimize postoperative edema. - Secondary Hemostasis for Persistent Oozing:
* If mild bleeding persists after 45 minutes, replace with a damp black tea bag wrapped in gauze and bite firmly for 30
minutes. Tannic acid in tea promotes local platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.

* For persistent socket bleeding: Inspect socket under good illumination. Clean excess liver clot with suction. Place topical
hemostatic agents:
- Oxidized regenerated cellulose (Surgicel) or absorbable gelatin sponge (Gelfoam) into socket. - Place figure-of-eight 3-0 or 4-0 resorbable suture (Vicryl or Chromic Gut) across the socket margins. - Local injection of 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine directly into surrounding gingival papillae for vasoconstriction.

* Topical Tranexamic Acid (TXA): 5% rinse (crush 500 mg tablet in 10 mL water) or soak gauze in TXA solution and hold
under pressure for 20 minutes. 2. MANAGEMENT OF PATIENTS ON ANTICOAGULANTS OR ANTIPLATELET THERAPY
- Warfarin (Coumadin): Check INR within 24 hours before procedure. * Therapeutic INR range between 2.0 and 3.0: Routine extractions can proceed safely without discontinuing Warfarin. Do
NOT stop Warfarin due to rebound thromboembolism risk.

* Use local hemostatic measures (Gelfoam/Surgicel, TXA mouthwash, primary closure with sutures). - Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs - Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Dabigatran):
* For standard single or simple extractions, DOAC discontinuation is generally unnecessary. * Schedule surgery 12 to 24 hours after last dose; next dose taken after definitive hemostasis achieved. - Antiplatelet Agents (Aspirin 81 mg, Clopidogrel 75 mg): Maintain therapy. Rely on local hemostatic agents. 3.

DRY SOCKET (ALVEOLAR OSTEITIS)
- Definition: Premature breakdown and fibrinolysis of blood clot within extraction socket, exposing alveolar bone and nerve
endings. - Incidence: 1-3% of routine extractions, up to 25-30% of impacted mandibular third molars.

[Page 2]
- Risk Factors: Tobacco smoking, oral contraceptives, difficult traumatic extraction, poor oral hygiene, female gender. - Clinical Presentation:
* Severe, throbbing, radiating pain developing 2 to 4 days post-operatively. * Pain often radiates to ear, temple, or eye. * Characteristic foul odor (halitosis), metallic bad taste, and visibly empty socket denuded of clot with exposed grayish bone. - Treatment Protocol:
1. Gently irrigate socket with warm sterile saline or 0.12% Chlorhexidine to flush necrotic food debris.

Do NOT aggressively
curette the bone, as this causes further bone trauma and delays healing. 2. Place a small sedating dressing: Zinc Oxide Eugenol paste on iodoform gauze or Alveogyl (eugenol-impregnated fiber
dressing). 3. Change dressing every 24 to 48 hours until pain resolves (usually 3 to 6 days). 4. Prescribe NSAIDs (Ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID with food) for analgesia. 5. Note: Antibiotics are NOT routinely indicated for dry socket unless there is spreading cellulitis, fever, or trismus.
